chapter.name: Number Play
chapter.blurb: Counting sequences from heights, parity of sums and expressions, row-and-column sum grids, magic squares, Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers and cryptarithms.

scope: Read the taller-in-front number a child calls out, write the numbers for a given height arrangement, and arrange heights to match a given number sequence
Decide whether statements about such sequences are always, only sometimes, or never true (first person says 0, tallest says 0, largest possible number in a group of n)
Use the pairing picture to find the parity of sums of even and odd numbers, including sums of many odd numbers
Use parity to decide whether a target sum is possible (number cards in boxes, ages of consecutive-year siblings, coin totals)
Find the parity of differences and of a product or grid of small squares from the parity of the factors
Decide the parity of an algebraic expression, build expressions that are always even, always odd or either, and use 2n and 2n - 1 as the nth even and odd numbers
Fill a 3 x 3 grid with 1 to 9 given row and column sums, and use the minimum sum 6, maximum sum 24 and total 45 to decide when a grid is impossible
Explain why a 3 x 3 magic square of 1 to 9 has magic sum 15 and centre 5, and why 1 and 9 cannot be in corners
Create magic squares from consecutive numbers, describe them with centre m, and see how adding to or multiplying every entry changes the magic sum
Recognise the 4 x 4 Chautisa Yantra with every row, column and diagonal summing to 34, and the 3 x 3 magic squares in Indian history
Count rhythms of short (1 beat) and long (2 beat) syllables, that is the ways to write n as a sum of 1s and 2s, and see that each count is the sum of the previous two
Extend the Virahanka-Fibonacci sequence forwards and backwards and find the pattern in its parities
Solve cryptarithms where each letter stands for one digit, using carrying and place-value reasoning
Modular arithmetic notation, divisibility tests or remainders after division by numbers other than 2 -- parity is the only such idea used here
Counting arrangements with factorials (for example the 3,62,880 ways to fill a 3 x 3 grid) -- the chapter says this comes in later years
Magic squares of order 5 or larger and general construction methods for them -- only mentioned as later-grade material
The closed-form formula, golden ratio or ratio-of-successive-terms property of Fibonacci numbers -- only the recurrence and the parity pattern are used
Formal induction or two-column proofs of parity rules -- the chapter proves them only with the pairing pictures

concepts.name: Sequences from heights (taller-in-front rule)
concepts.description: Reading the number each child calls when every child says how many children in front of them are taller, building the sequence for an arrangement, and arranging heights to fit a sequence.
concepts.idea: A child's number depends only on the children standing in front of them, never on those behind.
concepts.rule: A child's number is the count of taller children in front; the first child and the tallest child always say 0; in a group of n children the largest possible number is n - 1.
concepts.example: Heights 140, 150, 145 cm from the front give the numbers 0, 0, 1.

concepts.name: Parity of sums, differences and products
concepts.description: Deciding whether a sum, difference or product is even or odd from the parity of the numbers combined, and using this to show a target total is impossible.
concepts.idea: Even numbers pair up with nothing left over; every odd number leaves one unpaired item.
concepts.rule: even + even = even, odd + odd = even, even + odd = odd, and subtraction follows the same table; a sum of k odd numbers is odd when k is odd and even when k is even; a product is odd only when every factor is odd.
concepts.example: Five odd number cards can never add up to 30, because a sum of five odd numbers is odd.

concepts.name: Parity of expressions and the nth even and odd number
concepts.description: Deciding whether an algebraic expression is always even, always odd or sometimes either, and writing the nth even and odd numbers.
concepts.idea: In an expression, a term with an even multiplier is always even, so only the terms that can be odd decide the parity.
concepts.rule: 2n is the nth even number and 2n - 1 is the nth odd number; an expression like 3n + 4 can be odd or even because 3n changes parity with n.
concepts.example: 4m - 1 is odd for every whole number m, but 3n + 4 is odd for n = 3 and even for n = 8.

concepts.name: Row-and-column sum grids
concepts.description: Filling a 3 x 3 grid with the numbers 1 to 9 so the row and column sums match given circled values, and deciding when no such grid exists.
concepts.idea: Every number from 1 to 9 is used exactly once, so the row sums together and the column sums together each use all nine numbers.
concepts.rule: The three row sums add to 45 and so do the three column sums; any row or column sum must lie between 6 and 24.
concepts.example: A grid with a row sum of 5 is impossible because the smallest possible row sum is 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

concepts.name: Magic squares
concepts.description: Building and reasoning about 3 x 3 magic squares, including the magic sum, the centre number, the corners, generalising with a centre letter-number m, and the 4 x 4 Chautisa Yantra.
concepts.idea: In a magic square every row, column and diagonal has the same total, which forces the centre and the magic sum.
concepts.rule: A 3 x 3 magic square using 1 to 9 has magic sum 15 and centre 5; with centre m and nine consecutive numbers the magic sum is 3m; adding k to every entry adds 3k to the magic sum and multiplying every entry by k multiplies it by k.
concepts.example: Adding 1 to every number of the 1 to 9 magic square gives a magic square of 2 to 10 with magic sum 18.

concepts.name: Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers
concepts.description: Counting ways to write a number as a sum of 1s and 2s (rhythms of short and long syllables), extending the sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, and reading its parity pattern.
concepts.idea: Every rhythm of n beats starts with a 1 or a 2, so the count for n is the count for n - 1 plus the count for n - 2.
concepts.rule: The sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, ... adds the two previous terms; its parities repeat as odd, even, odd, odd, even, odd.
concepts.example: There are 8 ways to write 5 as a sum of 1s and 2s, because 5 beats gives 5 (from 4 beats) plus 3 (from 3 beats).

concepts.name: Cryptarithms (digits in disguise)
concepts.description: Solving addition puzzles in which each letter stands for one digit, using units-place, carrying and place-value reasoning.
concepts.idea: Different letters stand for different digits and the same letter always stands for the same digit, so each column of the sum limits the choices.
concepts.rule: Start from the units column, track the carry into the next column, and remember that the leading digit of a number cannot be 0.
concepts.example: In T + T + T = UT, only T = 5 works, giving 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 so U = 1.
